title: Classification of Commercial Organisations
tagline: Classifying organisations by activity, objective and ownership, with the industrial groupings and profit and non-profit distinctions the syllabus names.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original BoardPrep study material written against the CISCE ICSE Commercial Applications syllabus registered in this subject’s baseline (Examination Year 2027 and 2028 documents as reproduced by AglaSem, Scribd and Oswal Publishers; cisce.org returned 403). No board examination paper was consulted, every question is original practice, no figure is presented as an official statistic, and — as the syllabus itself requires — no question asks the student to record accounting entries or perform accounting calculations.

overview.intro: Unit 1(b) asks students to classify commercial organisations three ways: by the activities they perform, by their objectives, and by their ownership structures. Each lens answers a different question — what the organisation does, why it exists, and who owns it — and a complete answer says which lens it is using before it classifies. The syllabus requires industrial groupings such as textile and FMCG to be used as examples, the profit and non-profit objectives to be contrasted, and each ownership structure to be introduced with its features and distinctions. This chapter works through the three lenses in order, then classifies four real organisations across all of them so the student can see that classification is a tool, not a label.

learningOutcomes: Classify a commercial organisation by its activity, its objective and its ownership.
Explain the industrial groupings of textile and FMCG with examples.
Distinguish profit-making from non-profit organisations by purpose and by use of surplus.
Introduce each ownership structure with its features and its distinctions from the others.
Choose the correct lens for a given classification question.

learn.title: Classification by activity: what the organisation does

blocks.text: The first lens sorts organisations by the economic activity they perform. Primary organisations extract from nature — farming, fishing, mining and forestry; secondary organisations convert those extracts into usable goods — manufacturing, processing and construction; tertiary organisations provide services rather than goods — transport, banking, insurance and retail. Within the secondary grouping the syllabus names two industrial families that students must be able to use. The textile grouping gathers firms whose common thread is the fibre they handle: spinning mills, weaving units, knitting houses and garment exporters all sit in one family because cotton or jute moves through each of them on its way to cloth. The FMCG grouping gathers firms making fast-moving consumer goods — soaps, detergents, packaged foods, biscuits, shaving blades and cosmetics — whose shared features are low unit price, frequent purchase and wide distribution. The two groupings matter commercially because firms within one family compete for the same raw materials, the same shelf space and the same customers, which is why trade associations, advertising and pricing patterns cluster by grouping.

learn.title: Classification by objective: why the organisation exists

blocks.text: The second lens ignores activity and asks purpose. Profit-making organisations exist to earn a surplus for their owners, and every decision — what to produce, what to charge, where to open — is measured against that surplus. Non-profit organisations exist for a cause: a hospital trust, a school society, a sports club or a charitable foundation provides a service whose value is judged by the service itself, not by earnings. Three distinctions carry the marks. First, ownership of surplus: a profit firm distributes it as dividend or retains it for growth, while a non-profit organisation ploughs any surplus back into the cause. Second, motive for starting: a profit firm begins where return is visible, a non-profit begins where a need is unmet. Third, measure of success: one reports profit, the other reports reach — patients treated, students educated, members served. The syllabus also requires the caution that a non-profit may still charge fees and hold reserves; what makes it non-profit is the purpose, not the absence of money.

blocks.caption: Profit-making against non-profit organisations
rows: A FMCG company selling packaged foods

items.text: A school society charges fees yet remains non-profit, because no surplus is distributed to anyone.
items.note: Money flows through the organisation; the purpose decides the classification.

items.text: A cooperative dairy sells milk at competitive prices and returns profit to its farmer members.
items.note: Ownership-based classification cuts across the objective lens — it is a cooperative as well as a business.

learn.title: Classification by ownership: who owns the organisation

blocks.text: The third lens asks who holds the organisation and who bears its risk. A sole proprietorship is owned by one person who supplies the capital, runs the business and takes the whole profit and the whole loss; it is quick to start and private, but its owner’s liability is unlimited and its capital is limited by one person’s savings. A partnership is owned by two or more persons who agree to share profits under the Partnership Act; it brings more capital and wider skill, yet every general partner can be held responsible for the firm’s debts and disagreements can dissolve it. A joint stock company is incorporated: it raises capital by issuing shares, its shareholders’ liability stops at their investment, and its separate legal personality lets it sue, own property and continue through share transfers. A co-operative society is owned and controlled by its members on the principle of one member one vote, exists to serve members rather than outside investors, and is registered under co-operative law. The syllabus asks for the features and the distinctions of each, so every ownership answer should carry formation, liability, control and continuity before it names an example.

learn.title: Applying all three lenses to one organisation

blocks.text: Classification becomes examinable when the three lenses are applied to the same case, because each lens gives a different and equally correct answer. Take a cooperative sugar mill: by activity it is secondary industry, converting sugarcane into sugar; by objective it serves its farmer members by paying a fair cane price and returning surplus to them, so its purpose is member service; by ownership it is a co-operative, controlled one member one vote. Take instead a listed FMCG company: by activity it is secondary and belongs to the FMCG grouping; by objective it is profit-making; by ownership it is a joint stock company. A student who answers only one lens loses marks because the question names three bases of classification. The working rule is simple — read the question’s opening word. “Classify by activity” means primary, secondary or tertiary and, where relevant, the industrial grouping. “By objective” means profit or non-profit. “By ownership” means the four structures. If the question says “classify”, all three belong, in order, each with its own example.

items: Lens 1 — activity: what is produced or served, and which industrial grouping it belongs to.
Lens 2 — objective: profit-making or non-profit, judged by purpose and use of surplus.
Lens 3 — ownership: proprietorship, partnership, company or co-operative.
Always state the lens before classifying; an unlabelled answer cannot show the examiner which basis is being used.

keyPoints: Organisations may be classified by activity, by objective or by ownership — always name the lens first.
By activity: primary extracts, secondary converts, tertiary services.
The textile grouping spans spinning, weaving, knitting and garment firms handling the same fibres.
The FMCG grouping makes low-price, frequently purchased goods with wide distribution.
By objective: a profit organisation distributes or reinvests surplus for return; a non-profit reinvests it in its cause.
A non-profit may still charge fees — purpose, not the presence of money, decides the class.
Sole proprietorship: one owner, unlimited liability, no registration.
Partnership: shared capital and skill, but general partners answer for debts personally.
Joint stock company: incorporated, limited liability, separate legal personality.
Co-operative: owned by members on the principle of one member one vote.
examFocus: “Classify commercial organisations on the basis of ownership” — four headings, features of each, one example apiece.
“Distinguish profit-making from non-profit organisations” — purpose, use of surplus and measure of success.
“What is an FMCG grouping?” — define fast-moving consumer goods, list the shared features, then give two product examples.

vocabulary.meaning: Sorting organisations into groups according to a stated basis — activity, objective or ownership.
Economic activity that extracts products directly from nature.
Activity that converts raw or semi-finished materials into finished goods.
Service activity that supports production and trade without making goods.
Fast-moving consumer goods — low-priced products bought frequently and distributed widely.
An organisation formed to serve a cause, with any surplus reinvested rather than distributed.
A business owned and run by one person who bears unlimited liability.
A voluntary association owned and controlled by members on a one-member-one-vote basis.

questions.prompt: On the basis of objective, a charitable hospital trust is classified as:
questions.explanation: Its purpose is service rather than earnings, and any surplus is used to extend the service instead of being distributed — the test the objective lens applies.
questions.commonMistake: Its legal form may be a trust, but the question asks for classification by objective.

questions.prompt: Spinning mills, weaving units and garment exporters form one grouping because they:
options: Handle the same fibre on its way to cloth
Are all owned by one proprietor
questions.answer: Handle the same fibre on its way to cloth
questions.explanation: The textile grouping is defined by the common raw material and market the firms share, which is why they compete for the same inputs and customers.
questions.commonMistake: Groupings rest on activity, not on ownership or size.

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly matches an industrial grouping to its products?
questions.explanation: Fast-moving consumer goods are low-priced, frequently replaced items such as soaps, biscuits and packaged foods; cement, steel, transport and banking belong to other groupings entirely.
questions.commonMistake: Keep the two named groupings distinct: textile works with fibres, FMCG with everyday consumables.

questions.prompt: The clearest distinction between profit-making and non-profit organisations is:
options: How the surplus is used and what the organisation is measured by
How many employees the organisation has
Whether it sells goods or services
Whether it operates in more than one location
questions.answer: How the surplus is used and what the organisation is measured by
questions.explanation: A profit organisation distributes or reinvests its surplus for return and is measured by profit; a non-profit reinvests surplus in its cause and is measured by reach and service quality.
questions.commonMistake: Both may charge fees and both may employ hundreds — activity and size do not classify by objective.

questions.prompt: An organisation that extracts products directly from nature is called a ______ activity.
questions.explanation: Primary activities take resources straight from nature — farming, fishing, mining and forestry — before any conversion takes place.
questions.commonMistake: Do not write “tertiary”; tertiary organisations render services rather than extracting materials.

questions.prompt: State two features of a sole proprietorship and one reason it is limited in the capital it can raise.
questions.answer: Two features: it is owned and controlled by one person, and it requires no registration to begin. It is limited in capital because it can only use that one person’s savings and borrowings, with no issue of shares to the public.
questions.explanation: The features describe ownership and formation, while the capital limit follows directly from having a single owner — the connection the second half of the question demands.
questions.commonMistake: Unlimited liability is also a feature, but the capital point needs the single-owner cause stated.

questions.prompt: Explain why a cooperative society is classified separately from a profit-making company.
questions.answer: A cooperative is owned and controlled by its members on the principle of one member one vote, and exists to serve members rather than outside investors, so any surplus goes back to them. A company is owned by shareholders whose votes depend on shares held and exists to earn profit for them. The purpose and the control structure therefore differ, even though both may charge for what they provide.
questions.explanation: The answer compares the two on the two bases that actually separate them — control and purpose — rather than on superficial features such as registration.
questions.commonMistake: Both are registered bodies; registration alone cannot be the distinction.

questions.prompt: Classify a listed firm that manufactures biscuits and sells them through distributors, on the basis of activity, objective and ownership.
questions.answer: By activity: it is a secondary organisation, because it converts flour, sugar and other materials into finished biscuits; within that it belongs to the FMCG grouping, since biscuits are low-priced, frequently purchased and widely distributed. By objective: it is profit-making, as it manufactures to earn a surplus for its shareholders and measures success by profit. By ownership: it is a joint stock company, incorporated under company law, with shareholders whose liability is limited to their holdings and control exercised through an elected board. Each lens gives a different, valid classification of the same firm.
questions.explanation: All three lenses are applied in order, each with its reason and the required examples, which is what a three-mark classification question expects.
questions.commonMistake: Do not stop after one lens when the question names three bases.

questions.prompt: Explain the formation, liability and control of a partnership, and state one way it differs from a sole proprietorship.
questions.answer: Formation: a partnership is created by an agreement between two or more persons to carry on business and share profits, oral or written and optionally registered. Liability: every general partner is personally responsible for the firm’s debts, so the firm’s creditors can reach the partners’ personal property. Control: partners share management according to their agreement, each ordinarily having a say in running the business. Difference from a sole proprietorship: a partnership pools capital, skill and decision-making across several owners, whereas a sole proprietorship has one owner who alone supplies capital, alone controls the business and alone bears unlimited liability.
questions.explanation: Each heading is answered for the partnership and the closing sentence draws the contrast with a single-owner firm, which is the structure the question requests.
questions.commonMistake: Partnership liability is unlimited for general partners — do not confuse it with a company’s limited liability.

questions.prompt: A village formed a dairy society that collects milk from member farmers, sells it in town and returns the surplus to the members. Classify it on all three bases, and justify why the profit it earns does not make it a profit-making organisation.
questions.answer: By activity: it is a tertiary organisation, because it performs the service of collection, marketing and distribution rather than manufacturing; the collection centre also has a trading element when it sells in town. By objective: it is non-profit — the purpose is to secure a fair price for member farmers, and the surplus earned in the market is returned to the members rather than distributed as return on outside capital. By ownership: it is a co-operative, owned by its member farmers and controlled on the principle of one member one vote. Earning profit does not change the classification, because the objective lens asks what the surplus is for and who receives it: here the surplus returns to the very people who own and use the society, so it funds the cause instead of rewarding external investors. Profit is thus an outcome, not the objective, and classification follows the objective.
questions.explanation: The answer classifies under all three named bases, then attacks the apparent contradiction directly — surplus versus purpose — which is the reasoning the question is really testing.
questions.commonMistake: Do not classify it as profit-making merely because it sells at a price; the use of the surplus decides.
